config.title: Longest Consecutive Sequence

intro.title: Longest Consecutive Sequence
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a function that finds the length of the longest consecutive sequence of numbers in an unsorted array. You will learn the core concept of using a hash set for efficient lookups to solve this lesson without sorting. The main technologies involved are JavaScript arrays, the Set object, and basic loops and conditionals. By the end, you will understand how to implement an O(n) time complexity solution by checking for sequence starts and counting consecutive elements.
intro.usecase: The Longest Consecutive Sequence algorithm is essential for analyzing sequential data patterns in real-world applications. In e-commerce dashboards, it helps identify the longest streak of consecutive daily purchases by a customer to personalize loyalty rewards. Social media platforms use it to find users' longest consecutive login streaks for gamification features. Data analytics tools apply it to detect the longest uninterrupted sequence of sensor readings in IoT monitoring systems, highlighting periods of consistent operation.

objectives: Implement a function that finds the longest consecutive sequence in an array of integers
Apply a hash set data structure to efficiently check for consecutive elements
Construct an algorithm that iterates through array elements to identify sequence starting points
Manipulate array data by sorting or using alternative approaches to solve the lesson
Initialize and update variables to track the current sequence length and maximum length
Integrate conditional logic to handle edge cases like empty arrays and duplicate values
Configure test cases to validate the function's correctness with various input scenarios

content.body: Have you ever looked at a messy list of numbers and wondered: what's the longest chain of consecutive numbers hidden in there? Today we'll find exactly that. We'll learn how to spot consecutive sequences efficiently using a clever lookup technique.
content.title: Introduction

content.body:
By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to:
1. Explain why checking every possible sequence is inefficient
2. Implement a lookup structure to track seen numbers
3. Build the longest consecutive sequence algorithm step by step
4. Determine when to check versus when to add to your lookup
5. Return the correct length of the longest sequence
content.title: What you'll learn
Try it
content.prompt: In this array: [3, 1, 4], what's the longest chain of consecutive numbers? (Example: 1,2,3 is consecutive)
content.successMessage: Nice! The numbers 3 and 4 are consecutive, and 1 is separate, so the longest chain is length 2.

content.title: Try a bigger array
content.prompt: Now with [100, 4, 200, 1, 3, 2], what's the longest consecutive chain?
content.successMessage: Well done! 1, 2, 3, 4 form a chain of length 4. 100 and 200 are separate.

content.title: One more
content.successMessage: Great! You found the chain 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 of length 9. You probably checked numbers one by one to build sequences.

content.body: What you just did was a form of brute force: you looked at each number and tried to build sequences from it. For small arrays, this works, but it involves repeatedly checking if numbers exist in the array.
content.title: What you did

content.body: When the array has 10,000 numbers, building sequences from each number becomes extremely slow. We'd be doing the same lookups over and over. We need a way to remember what we've already seen and avoid re-scanning. Can't figure it out? Click Show me on the next step.
content.title: Why it gets hard

content.body: The core idea is: remember what we have already seen. Instead of scanning the array repeatedly, we can use a lookup structure (like a Set) to instantly check if a number exists. Think of it as a notebook where we write down all the numbers once, then we can check any number in one step without searching through the array again.
content.title: Key idea
content.visualMetaphor: A notebook where we write down what we've seen and check it in one step.

content.body: We'll use a single pass to store all numbers in a Set for instant lookup. Then, for each number, we check if it's the start of a sequence (by seeing if the number-1 exists). If it is, we count how many consecutive numbers follow using our Set. This way, each number is processed at most twice.
content.title: The approach
content.illustratedExample:
Walkthrough with [100, 4, 200, 1, 3, 2]:
1. Create Set with all numbers: {100, 4, 200, 1, 3, 2}
2. Check 100: Is 99 in Set? No → start sequence at 100
   Count: 100 (length 1), 101 not in Set → stop
3. Check 4: Is 3 in Set? Yes → skip (not start of sequence)
4. Check 200: Is 199 in Set? No → start sequence at 200
   Count: 200 (length 1), 201 not in Set → stop
5. Check 1: Is 0 in Set? No → start sequence at 1
   Count: 1, 2, 3, 4 (length 4), 5 not in Set → stop
6. Longest sequence length = 4

content.body:
1. Create a Set from all numbers in the array (our 'notebook' of seen numbers)
2. Initialize a variable to track the longest sequence length
3. For each number in the Set:
   a. Check if it's the start of a sequence (number-1 is NOT in the Set)
   b. If yes, count how many consecutive numbers follow (number+1, number+2, etc.)
   c. Update the longest length if this sequence is longer
4. Return the longest length
content.title: Steps

steps.title: Create the function skeleton
steps.instruction: Start by creating a function called longestConsecutive that takes a nums array as parameter. Return 0 for now.
steps.hint: Remember function syntax: function name(parameter) { return value; }
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've set up the function structure.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost there. Make sure you're returning 0 from the function.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. Create a function called longestConsecutive that takes nums and returns 0.

steps.title: Handle edge case: empty array
steps.instruction: At the beginning of your function, check if nums is empty. If it is, return 0 immediately.
steps.hint: Use an if statement: if (nums.length === 0) return 0;
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You're handling the edge case properly.
steps.feedbackPartial: Check your condition. It should return 0 when the array has no elements.
steps.feedbackWrong: Remember: if nums has no elements (length is 0), we should return 0 immediately.

steps.title: Create the Set lookup
steps.instruction: Create a Set from the nums array. This will be our 'notebook' of all numbers we've seen.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Excellent! Now we have instant lookup for any number.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost. You need to create a Set containing all elements from nums.
steps.feedbackWrong: Create a Set using new Set(nums) to store all numbers for quick lookup.

steps.title: Initialize tracking variables
steps.instruction: Create a variable called longest to track the maximum sequence length, starting at 0.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Good! We'll use this to track our answer.
steps.feedbackPartial: You need to declare a variable to store the longest sequence length.
steps.feedbackWrong: Create a variable named longest and set it to 0 to track the maximum length.

steps.title: Find sequences and update longest
steps.instruction: Loop through the Set. For each number, check if it's the start of a sequence (num-1 not in Set). If yes, count consecutive numbers and update longest.
steps.hint: Use for...of loop, check !numSet.has(num-1), then while loop to count forward.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Fantastic! You've implemented the complete algorithm.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're checking for sequence starts and counting forward.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try this structure: loop through numSet, if num-1 doesn't exist, count how many consecutive numbers follow, update longest.

content.body:
Congratulations! You've implemented the Longest Consecutive Sequence algorithm. Remember the key insights:
1. Use a Set for O(1) lookups instead of scanning the array repeatedly
2. Only start counting from numbers that are sequence starters (when num-1 doesn't exist)
3. Each number is processed at most twice, making this O(n) efficient

This 'remember what we've seen' pattern with lookup structures is powerful for many array lessons!
